correct_citation: Bos, J. M., Dhillon, S., & Borman, T. (2019). Building Assets and Reducing Risks (BARR) Validation Study: Final Report. American Institutes for Research (ERIC ED602462).
design: Random assignment of ninth-grade students to BARR or control within schools; one-year impacts (i3 validation).
population_location: Ninth graders in 11 high schools in Maine, California, Minnesota, Kentucky and Texas.
outcome: Failed at least one core course; GPA; NWEA MAP reading/math; student experiences; chronic absence, suspensions, persistence into 10th grade.
effect_as_reported: Failed >=1 core course 29.2% vs 40.6% (-11.5 pp, ES 0.31, significant); GPA 2.58 vs 2.48 (+0.10, ES 0.11, significant); chronic absence 23.1% vs 21.9% (n.s.); no credit-accrual impact reported; graduation not measured.
excerpt: BARR significantly reduced course failure and increased students’ GPA at the end of ninth grade.
note: Course failure and GPA confirmed. The claimed significant gain in credits toward graduation is not in the report: core credits were collected only to derive course failure and GPA, and no credit impact is estimated. Graduation was not measured (one-year study; persistence into 10th grade n.s.). BARR had no significant effect on attendance or chronic absence.

correct_citation: Faria, A.-M., Sorensen, N., Heppen, J., Bowdon, J., Taylor, S., Eisner, R., & Foster, S. (2017). Getting Students on Track for Graduation: Impacts of the Early Warning Intervention and Monitoring System after One Year (REL 2017-272). REL Midwest (ERIC ED573814).
design: School-level randomized trial: 73 high schools (37 EWIMS, 36 control), 2014/15.
population_location: 37,671 first- and second-year high school students in three Midwest Region states.
outcome: Chronic absence (missed >=10% of instructional time); failed >=1 course; low GPA; suspension; insufficient credits to be on track.
effect_as_reported: Chronic absence 10% vs 14% (-4 pp, significant); course failure 21% vs 26% (-5 pp, significant); low GPA and suspension n.s.; insufficient credits 14% in both (n.s.); graduation and dropout not examined.
excerpt: The percentage of students who were chronically absent (missed 10 percent or more of instructional time) was lower in EWIMS schools (10 percent) than in control schools (14 percent); this 4 percentage point difference was statistically significant.
note: Given URL is Semantic Scholar; primary is ERIC ED573814. The report says dropout and on-time graduation could not be examined. There was no credit effect.

correct_citation: Sletten, M. A., Tøge, A. G., & Malmberg-Heimonen, I. (2023). Effects of an early warning system on student absence and completion in Norwegian upper secondary schools: a cluster-randomised study. Scandinavian Journal of Educational Research, 67(7), 1151-1165 (online 2022). https://doi.org/10.1080/00313831.2022.2116481
design: Cluster-randomised trial of the IKO early warning model: 20 schools experimental, 22 control; two-level regression on administrative data.
population_location: 7,677 first-year students in 42 Norwegian upper secondary schools.
outcome: Absence from lectures, completion rates, academic results after two school years.
effect_as_reported: No significant effects on absence, completion or academic results; no stronger effects for students at risk.
excerpt: After two school years, there were no significant effects on absence from lectures, completion rates, or academic results.
note: Publisher abstract fetched via OpenAlex (Taylor & Francis page blocked). Online first 2022; issue 2023, vol. 67, pp. 1151-1165.

correct_citation: Lass, K., Walsh, S., Burgess, K., Kuperberg Levin, J., & Jenner, E. (2025). Achievement Mentoring: Final Evaluation Report. The Policy & Research Group (June 2025; ERIC ED676904).
design: Individual-level RCT, ITT; three cohorts 2021-22 to 2023-24 (EIR grant).
population_location: 393 10th- and 11th-grade students in five Eastern states, eligible by a 9th-grade risk flag (20+ days missed, failed core course, or 3+ disciplinary infractions).
outcome: Days attended, credits earned, suspension (school records); social-emotional survey measures.
effect_as_reported: 10th grade: days attended 147.91 vs 146.19 (+1.72, p=.432, g=0.06); credits 8.03 vs 7.37 (+0.67, p=.196, g=0.10); suspended 20.1% vs 30.1% (p=.036, Cox -0.44). End of 11th grade: days attended -9.44 (p=.165, g=-0.17); credits +0.83 (p=.432, g=0.06); suspension +0.02 (p=.757). Graduation and dropout not measured.
excerpt: offering one-on-one mentoring through the AM program for one year had a statistically significant effect on students’ likelihood of getting suspended in 10th grade (p = 0.036), but not on their school attendance or credit accrual rate (p > 0.10).
note: ERIC has no full text; the report came from the PRG site. Graduation is discussed only as an aspiration. In the subgroup analysis, non-rural schools showed more days attended and credits.

correct_citation: Hemelt, S. W., Lenard, M. A., & Paeplow, C. G. (2019). Building bridges to life after high school: Contemporary career academies and student outcomes. Economics of Education Review, 68, 161-178 (CALDER WP 176, 2017, "Building Better Bridges to Life after High School: Experimental Evidence on Contemporary Career Academies", ERIC ED572934).
design: Lottery-based admission to one technology-focused career academy (causal estimates using lottery).
population_location: Wake County Public School System, North Carolina.
outcome: High school graduation, college enrollment, 9th-grade absences, achievement, AP.
effect_as_reported: Graduation and college enrollment each up about 8 percentage points (about 9% of control mean), gains concentrated among males; reduced 9th-grade absences; about one fifth of the graduation effect is attributed to engagement or absences.
excerpt: We find that enrollment in this academy increases the likelihood of high school graduation and college enrollment each by about 8 percentage points, with the attainment gains concentrated among male students.
note: Journal citation confirmed via Crossref (10.1016/j.econedurev.2018.08.005). The working-paper title differs slightly from the claim.

correct_citation: Neild, R. C., Boccanfuso, C., & Byrnes, V. (2015). Academic Impacts of Career and Technical Schools. Career and Technical Education Research, 40(1), 28-47 (ERIC EJ1132478). https://doi.org/10.5328/cter40.1.28
design: Natural experiment: randomized admission lottery to CTE schools; admitted vs not-admitted lottery applicants (ITT and dosage estimates).
population_location: Classes of 2003-2005, School District of Philadelphia CTE high schools.
outcome: Graduation, credit accumulation, college-prep math sequence; science and foreign-language sequences, GPA, math and reading achievement.
effect_as_reported: CTE students had significantly better graduation, credit accumulation and math sequence completion; other outcomes inconsistent across cohorts.
excerpt: Results find that CTE students had significantly better outcomes in terms of graduation rates, credit accumulation, and the successful completion of the college preparatory mathematics sequence algebra 1, algebra 2, and geometry.
note: Admission was by randomized lottery (with race balancing, per the 2013 report ED611156). The journal title in Crossref has no subtitle; "A Case Study of a Large Urban School District" is the subtitle of the 2013 CSOS report. Effect sizes were not available (the abstract gives none; full text was not fetched).

correct_citation: Plasman, J., Stein, M. L., Durham, R. E., & Smith-Onyewu, Z. (2025). CTE Mechanisms: The Effects of Career and Technical Education Center Admissions Offers in Baltimore. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, 47(3), 682-702 (online 2024). https://doi.org/10.3102/01623737241239299
design: Regression discontinuity at a strict admissions cut score.
population_location: Baltimore City Public Schools CTE-focused high schools.
outcome: Attendance, CTE pathway completion, high school GPA, SAT scores.
effect_as_reported: Offer of admission: significantly more likely to complete a CTE pathway; significantly lower GPAs. The abstract gives no attendance or graduation estimate.
excerpt: We find that students who are offered admission to a program within one of the CTE centers are significantly more likely to complete a CTE pathway, though they present significantly lower GPAs.
note: Design, population and the pathway/GPA direction confirmed from the publisher abstract. The full text (Sage) was blocked, so the attendance result and any graduation estimate could not be checked. A search snippet suggests attendance was n.s., but that is unverified.

correct_citation: Wills, T. W., Wolford, T. E., & Goldberg, A. (2017). Effects of Career and Technical Education on Graduation Rates: A Longitudinal Study from the School District of Philadelphia. Paper presented at AERA, San Antonio (ERIC ED603343).
design: Longitudinal correlational analysis controlling for academic, behavioral and demographic factors.
population_location: 2011-12 first-time 9th-grade cohort, School District of Philadelphia.
outcome: Graduation outcomes over four years.
effect_as_reported: CTE participation associated with higher graduation; protective effect extends to students entering 10th grade with strongest predictors of failure. No size in abstract.
excerpt: participation in CTE was associated with higher graduation outcomes, controlling for academic, behavioral and demographic factors known to influence graduation.
note: Only the ERIC abstract is reachable (no ERIC full text; AERA repository not located). Not confirmed: the effect size, whether prior achievement and attendance are controls, and the "four-year graduation" wording. ERIC tags it as correlational.

correct_citation: Glennie, E., Dalton, B., Studley, R., & Lauff, E. (2025). The Influence of Earning Industry Certifications on High School Graduation: Evidence from Florida. Educational Policy, 39, 1241-1270 (online 2024; ERIC EJ1476967). https://doi.org/10.1177/08959048241292625
design: Described only as a quasi-experimental design examining the association.
population_location: Florida high school students.
outcome: On-time high school graduation.
effect_as_reported: Certifications exert a meaningful influence on likelihood of graduation; stronger for students at risk of dropping out or economically disadvantaged. No size in abstract.
excerpt: Our findings indicate that certifications exert a meaningful influence on the likelihood of high school graduation, and that the effect is stronger for students who are at risk for dropping out or are economically disadvantaged.
note: Direction and subgroups confirmed. The full text (Sage) was blocked, so the specific method, any prior-achievement adjustment and the size are unverified. The authors frame the result as an association.

correct_citation: Castellano, M. E., Richardson, G. B., Sundell, K., & Stone, J. R. III (2017). Preparing Students for College and Career in the United States: The Effects of Career-Themed Programs of Study on High School Performance. Vocations and Learning, 10, 47-70 (online 2016; ERIC EJ1133891). https://doi.org/10.1007/s12186-016-9162-7
design: Structural equations with an instrumental-variable approach.
population_location: US high school students in career-themed programs of study (districts not named in abstract).
outcome: Graduation and high school GPA.
effect_as_reported: POS enrollment raised probability of graduation by 11.3%; each additional CTE credit in POS +4%; GPA effects non-significant.
excerpt: Results indicated that POS enrollment improved students’ probability of graduation by 11.3% and that each additional CTE credit earned in POS increased their probability of graduation by 4%.
note: IV design and graduation size confirmed. Not confirmed: the "two districts" (Springer page blocked) and test scores as an outcome (the abstract lists only GPA and graduation). The paper uses IV, not a lottery.

correct_citation: Furstenberg, F. F., Jr., & Neumark, D. (2007). Encouraging Education in an Urban School District: Evidence from the Philadelphia Educational Longitudinal Study. Education Economics, 15(2), 135-157 (ERIC EJ764115; NBER WP 11260, 2005).
design: Linear models and propensity score matching using extensive pre-placement data (PELS).
population_location: Philadelphia high school students in school-to-career and college-encouragement programs.
outcome: High school dropout and graduation; awards; college attitudes and attendance.
effect_as_reported: Positive effects on graduation; STC participation reduces probability of dropping out by about 5-6 percentage points; graduation significantly and sizably higher (robust to test-score controls).
excerpt: The magnitude of the estimated effect implies that participation in an STC program reduces the probability of dropping out by about five or six percentage points.
note: Graduation size checked via NBER WP text (Table 4 described as large and significant). The journal version was confirmed from the ERIC abstract.

correct_citation: Berger, A., Turk-Bicakci, L., Garet, M., Song, M., Knudson, J., Haxton, C., Zeiser, K., Hoshen, G., Ford, J., Stephan, J., Keating, K., & Cassidy, L. (2013). Early College, Early Success: Early College High School Initiative Impact Study. AIR (ERIC ED577243).
design: Lottery-based randomized experiment at 10 Early Colleges using admission lotteries.
population_location: 2,458 students, cohorts entering 9th grade 2005-06 to 2007-08.
outcome: High school graduation, college enrollment and degree attainment; ELA/math assessments.
effect_as_reported: 86% of Early College students graduated vs 81% of comparison students (significant).
excerpt: 86 percent of Early College students graduated from high school, which was significantly higher than the 81 percent for comparison students.

correct_citation: Glennie, E., Unlu, F., & Furey, J. (2016). The Small, Stand-Alone Early College: Impact on High School Outcomes. SREE (ERIC ED567039).
design: IES-funded longitudinal experimental study using lottery assignment of early college applicants.
population_location: North Carolina early college high school applicants.
outcome: College-prep course completion, college credits, five-year high school graduation (regular diploma).
effect_as_reported: Five-year graduation impact +3.1 percentage points, statistically significant.
excerpt: The overall impact on five-year graduation rates is 3.1 percentage points, which was statistically significant.
note: Content is right, but the document lists only Glennie, Unlu and Furey as authors (Edmunds, Bernstein, Fesler and Arshavsky are not on it). The outcome is five-year graduation.

correct_citation: Maxwell, N., Bellotti, J., Schochet, P., Burkander, P., Whitesell, E., Dillon, E., Inanc, H., Geckeler, C., & González, R. (2019). Building College and Career Pathways for High School Students: Youth CareerConnect. Impact Findings Report. Mathematica for U.S. DOL (ERIC ED618302; WWC study 90317).
design: RCT (WWC: meets standards without reservations), plus a separate QED using school records.
population_location: RCT: 436 students grades 9-12 in three districts (follow-up survey about two years after start).
outcome: Enrolled in high school, unexcused absences, cut class, late, credentials, employment, suspension.
effect_as_reported: RCT: no significant effects on any of 20 survey outcomes (e.g., unexcused absences 55.0 vs 55.3; enrolled in HS 94.0 vs 92.8; credential 26.9 vs 28.9).
excerpt: The RCT suggested that the YCC program did not affect any of the 20 outcomes captured by the follow-up survey
note: The RCT was underpowered. The report's primary QED found small significant gains in attendance (+0.7 pp of days present, 0.05 SD) and credits (0.11 SD), so the "no effect" claim applies to the RCT only.

correct_citation: Theodos, B., Pergamit, M. R., Hanson, D., Edelstein, S., & Daniels, R. (2016). Embarking on College and Career: Interim Evaluation of Urban Alliance. Urban Institute (ERIC ED570478).
design: Six-year randomized controlled trial; ITT and TOT estimates.
population_location: High school seniors in Washington, DC and Baltimore, 2011-12 and 2012-13 program years.
outcome: High school graduation, senior-year suspension, chronic absence, cumulative GPA.
effect_as_reported: Graduated HS 0.98 vs 0.96; ITT regression-adjusted +0.012 (SE 0.010), n.s.; males +4 pp, n.s. after multiple-comparison adjustment.
excerpt: We found no significant impacts under the ITT or TOT framework (table 9).
note: Content confirmed from the interim report. The citation conflates two reports: ED570478 is the 2016 interim report with five authors; Srini and the "final" evaluation belong to a separate 2017 report that was not checked.

correct_citation: Constantine, J. M., Seftor, N. S., Martin, E. S., Silva, T., & Myers, D. (2006). Study of the Effect of the Talent Search Program on Secondary and Postsecondary Outcomes in Florida, Indiana and Texas. U.S. Department of Education (ERIC ED493358).
design: Quasi-experimental propensity-score matched comparison on administrative records (WWC: meets standards with reservations).
population_location: Talent Search participants vs comparison students in Florida, Indiana and Texas (completion examined in FL and TX).
outcome: High school completion (diploma or GED), FAFSA application, college enrollment.
effect_as_reported: High school completion 9 pp higher in Florida (86% vs 77%) and 14 pp higher in Texas; WWC rates it a statistically significant positive finding (improvement index +19 FL) and potentially positive effects on completing school.
excerpt: There were large differences in Florida and Texas—9 and 14 percentage points, respectively—between Talent Search participants and nonparticipants.
note: The claim says there was no significant effect on HS completion, but the source and WWC both report a significant positive one. The authors caution that the completion estimate may be biased upward by unmeasured motivation and call it a possible upper bound.

correct_citation: Todhunter-Reid, A., Burke, A., Houchens, P., & Howard, M. (2020). AVID Participation in High School and Post-Secondary Success: An Evaluation and Cost Analysis. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, 13(4), 679-701 (ERIC EJ1275427). https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2020.1772421
design: Coarsened Exact Matching on 40 baseline characteristics; cost analysis by ingredients method.
population_location: AVID and non-AVID high school students (location not stated in abstract).
outcome: High school graduation and college enrollment.
effect_as_reported: Students completing at least one AVID elective had higher HS graduation and college enrollment rates; no size in abstract.
excerpt: Findings indicate that students who complete at least one AVID elective have higher high school graduation and college enrollment rates than comparable non-AVID students.
note: There are only four authors (no "et al."). The full text is closed access, so prior achievement among the 40 covariates and the effect size are unverified.

correct_citation: Sepanik, S., Safran, S., & Saco, L. (2018). Building College Readiness across Rural Communities: Implementation and Outcome Findings for the AVID Central Florida Collaborative Study. MDRC (ERIC ED582154).
design: Pre-post nonexperimental comparison within schools (no comparison schools); authors say it does not capture causation.
population_location: Four high schools and four middle schools in three rural central Florida districts.
outcome: Advanced course credits, GPA, ELA, total and core credits, promotion, graduation, persistence.
effect_as_reported: Graduation 85.7% pre vs 83.2% year 3 (-2.5, p=.383); total credits 5.15 vs 5.11 (n.s.); earned an advanced credit +8.0 pp (p<.001).
excerpt: Little difference in other measures of students’ academic performance (grade point average and English Language Arts standardized tests), educational attainment (overall credits earned and graduation), and high school persistence were found
note: The direction is right, but the design is wrong: the study is a pre-post comparison, not a comparative interrupted time series, and it has no comparison group.

correct_citation: Kim, H., Montague, M. L., & Castillo, L. G. (2025). The Effects of Gaining Early Awareness and Readiness for Undergraduate Programs on Educational Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis. Journal of Diversity in Higher Education, 18(S), S473-S481 (ERIC EJ1506317). https://doi.org/10.1037/dhe0000586
design: Random-effects meta-analysis of eight GEAR UP studies, plus proportional meta-analyses.
population_location: GEAR UP participants (historically underrepresented students).
outcome: Several educational outcomes, including ACT, attendance rate, college enrollment rate, graduation rate.
effect_as_reported: Effects ranged from small (ACT) to large (attendance rate); college enrollment and graduation rates higher for GEAR UP participants; no numeric sizes in abstract.
excerpt: Results of two proportional meta-analyses revealed that both college enrollment rate and graduation rate were higher for GEAR UP participants compared to non-GEAR UP participants.
note: Closed access, so the share of studies with a comparison group, the designs and the sizes are unverified. The abstract does not say "high school" graduation. Pooled proportions may not be comparison-group effects.

correct_citation: Miller, C., Cummings, D., Millenky, M., Wiegand, A., & Long, D. (2018). Laying a Foundation: Four-Year Results from the National YouthBuild Evaluation. MDRC (ERIC ED590015).
design: Random assignment impact evaluation at 75 programs.
population_location: Low-income out-of-school young people ages 16 to 24 who had not completed high school.
outcome: High school diploma or equivalency credential at 48 months (survey).
effect_as_reported: Diploma or equivalency 54.6% vs 45.7% (+8.9 pp***); equivalency 34.5% vs 23.5% (+11.0 pp***); diploma 20.1% vs 22.1% (-2.0, n.s.).
excerpt: YouthBuild led to a sizable increase in high school equivalency credential receipt.
note: The gain is entirely in equivalency credentials (GED/HSE). There was no diploma impact.

correct_citation: Millenky, M., Bloom, D., & Dillon, C. (2010). Making the Transition: Interim Results of the National Guard Youth ChalleNGe Evaluation. MDRC (ERIC ED514652).
design: Random assignment (lottery-like admission among qualified applicants); about 3,000 youths in 10 programs; survey about 21 months after entry.
population_location: 16- to 18-year-olds who had dropped out of high school.
outcome: Earned high school diploma or GED.
excerpt: the program’s impact was concentrated on GED receipt. Nevertheless, there was also a statistically significant increase in the percentage of sample members with a high school diploma.
note: The gains were mainly GEDs, with a smaller but significant diploma gain.

correct_citation: Cave, G., Bos, H., Doolittle, F., & Toussaint, C. (1993). JOBSTART: Final Report on a Program for School Dropouts. MDRC (ERIC ED363774).
design: Random assignment of 2,312 eligible applicants; 1,941 with 48-month follow-up.
population_location: Economically disadvantaged school dropouts aged 17-21 with poor reading skills, 13 sites.
outcome: Received high school diploma or GED within 48 months.
effect_as_reported: 42% vs 28.6%, a significant difference of 13.4 pp; mostly GEDs.
excerpt: By the end of the four years, 42 percent of experimentals had obtained a high school diploma or GED, as compared to 28.6 percent of controls, for a statistically significant difference of 13.4 percentage points.

correct_citation: Riccio, J., Dechausay, N., Miller, C., Nuñez, S., Verma, N., & Yang, E. (2013). Conditional Cash Transfers in New York City: The Continuing Story of the Opportunity NYC-Family Rewards Demonstration. MDRC (ERIC ED545453).
design: Randomized control trial of about 4,800 families.
population_location: New York City low-income families; high school students in the ninth-grade cohort.
outcome: Graduation within 4 years, credits, Regents exams.
effect_as_reported: Few effects for HS students overall (graduation 49.2 vs 48.2, n.s.); among 8th-grade-ELA-proficient students: graduation +8.0 pp (74.8 vs 66.9), on-track credits +9.6 pp, passed 5+ Regents +9.5 pp; math-proficient subgroup no graduation gain.
excerpt: Family Rewards had few effects on school outcomes for high school students overall. However, it substantially increased graduation rates and other outcomes for students who were already stronger readers.
note: The gains were only for students proficient at entry, not overall.

correct_citation: Miller, C., Miller, R., Verma, N., Dechausay, N., Yang, E., Rudd, T., Rodriguez, J., & Honig, S. (2016). Effects of a Modified Conditional Cash Transfer Program in Two American Cities: Findings from Family Rewards 2.0. MDRC (ERIC ED569137).
design: Randomized trial.
population_location: Families in the Bronx and Memphis.
outcome: School progress: grade progression, credits earned, on-time graduation, college entrance exams.
effect_as_reported: No effect on school progress through Year 4 for the full sample or the proficient subgroup (e.g., on-time graduation 63.4 vs 63.1, n.s.).
excerpt: The program did not affect students’ school progress through Year 4, either for the full sample of students or for the subgroup of academically proficient students.
note: Content is right, but James Riccio is not an author (he is only thanked), and the date is September 2016, not 2016-2017.

correct_citation: Long, D., Gueron, J. M., Wood, R. G., Fisher, R., & Fellerath, V. (1996). LEAP: Three-Year Impacts of Ohio's Welfare Initiative to Improve School Attendance among Teenage Parents. MDRC (ERIC ED396380).
design: Random assignment; three-year survey of 913 teens in 7 counties plus school records for 4,325.
population_location: Pregnant and parenting teens on welfare (AFDC) in Ohio.
outcome: Completed grade 11, ever completed high school, GED, high school or GED.
effect_as_reported: Full sample: completed grade 11 +4.6 pp (p<.10); HS or GED 34.0 vs 31.9 (+2.1, n.s.); GED +2.7 n.s. on survey but significant in school records. In-school teens: GED +5.6 pp**, HS or GED +7.0 (n.s.); dropouts: no gain. Cleveland: graduation rose substantially.
excerpt: For the full sample of teens, LEAP substantially increased high school enrollment, attendance, and progress through the eleventh grade, but did not have a significant impact on high school graduation.
note: "No significant effect on completion" holds only for full-sample HS/GED completion. LEAP raised grade-11 completion (marginal) and GED receipt for initially enrolled teens; the abstract cites about a 20% completion increase for them. A "dropped out" outcome was not found in the summary tables.
